You see things in black-and-white categories. If a situation falls short of perfect, you see it as a total failure.
You see a single negative event as part of a never-ending pattern, often using words like \"always\" or \"never\".
You dwell on a single negative detail so much that your view of reality becomes darkened, like a drop of ink coloring a glass of water.
You reject positive experiences by insisting they \"don\'t count\" for some reason.
You assume you know what someone else is thinking, without real evidence for it — and usually assume the worst.
You predict that things will turn out badly, and treat that prediction as if it were already an established fact.
You exaggerate the importance of problems and shortcomings, or shrink the importance of your good qualities.
You assume your negative emotions reflect the way things really are: \"I feel it, therefore it must be true.\"
You tell yourself things should be the way you hoped, using \"should,\" \"must,\" or \"ought to,\" which leaves you feeling guilty or resentful.
An extreme form of overgeneralization — instead of describing an error, you attach a fixed negative label to yourself or others.
You see yourself as the cause of some negative external event that you weren\'t primarily responsible for.
Why is living in fear of opposition and criticism irrational and unnecessary?
Tap + to write your first page on this topic. Come back and add more pages whenever a new thought about it occurs to you.

A few starting thoughts on this topic:

1. If someone reacts negatively to you, their reaction often says more about their own assumptions than about your worth.

2. If a criticism is accurate, that's not a catastrophe — you can note the error, correct it, and move on without deciding it makes you a bad person.

3. One mistake describes one moment, not your entire track record. You can keep changing after it.

4. Other people can only judge a specific thing you did or said — no one is in a position to grade you as a whole person.

5. No matter how well you do, someone will disagree with you. Disapproval doesn't spread on its own; one "no" isn't a verdict that follows you everywhere.

6. Discomfort after criticism is normal and temporary — it fades on its own without needing to be argued away.

7. Criticism mostly stings when you've quietly accepted the negative label behind it. Question the label, not just the sting.

8. Disagreement is an ordinary part of any relationship — it doesn't require the relationship to end.

9. Add your own idea here whenever one occurs to you — this list is yours to keep building.

This method, popularized by psychiatrist David Burns in \"Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy,\" is a simple way to talk back to upsetting thoughts. Write down the automatic thought as it occurred to you, identify which distortion(s) are twisting your thinking, then write a rational response that answers the thought fairly. Rating how much you believe the thought before and after helps you see the shift.
The Journal tab is a single-topic notebook dedicated to: “%1$s” Add a new dated page any time a fresh thought about it occurs to you — there\'s no limit to how many pages you keep.
